mutate_comment: The .ts layers (utils/hooks/use-cases/services) hold the app's logic and are mutation-tested wholesale. Components (.tsx) were previously excluded, but the three that gate a DESTRUCTIVE action (the delete confirmation, the database export/import/restore section, and the library folder section, which starts the move of the whole library) are worth mutating so a test change that stops actually exercising those flows is caught. They are named individually rather than by a src/components/**/*.tsx glob on purpose: a measured isolated run (2026-07-18) scored the first two at 56.25% (mutants dominated by UI-text/prop-detail that tests reasonably do not assert), so a blanket component glob would drag the aggregate down and pile un-actioned survivors into the report. Their mutants are a small fraction of the ~4.6k total, so the aggregate score stays ~71.5% (well above the break below). Widen this list only after measuring each candidate the same way.
library_folder_section_comment: Measured isolated on 2026-07-31 before being added, the same way the other two were. First pass: 72.97% total / 81.82% covered, 6 survivors. Three were the '-' placeholder string literals shown while a counter loads, the accepted UI-text class described above. The other three were all the one guard that renders the 'why you cannot change the folder' alert, and only one of those was a real gap. Nothing asserted the alert is ABSENT when the change is not blocked, so a guard weakened to always-true would leave a stale explanation under enabled buttons. A test for that direction took the file to 81.08% total / 90.91% covered with 3 survivors, all of them the string literals. That is the highest of the three components here and well clear of the break. WORTH KNOWING FOR THE NEXT CANDIDATE: the other two of those six were false survivors, not real ones. Re-running with coverageAnalysis 'all' killed them, and hand-applying one and running this component's own test file killed it too: perTest had attributed the mutant to HomeModals tests rather than to the direct test file. Do not chase a survivor on a .tsx here without first checking it by hand, and if a candidate ever measures poorly, confirm the survivors are real before rejecting it. Switching coverageAnalysis to 'all' repo-wide is not the answer. See the note below on why perTest exists.
repositories_comment: Added 2026-08-02 after a measured isolated run, following the protocol above: 95.24% total / 100% covered, 20 killed, 0 survivors, in a scope of 21 mutants. It goes in clean. These are the thin typed layer directly over a database-backed Tauri command (one function per command, no business logic), so the scope is small by construction, and what it pins is the part that is easy to get wrong precisely because there is nothing else there: the command name each function names and the argument object it builds. A renamed argument is a command receiving undefined, which is not a type error on either side of the IPC boundary. The one mutant with no coverage is the ObjectLiteral in list_media_page's argument, whose emptied form the page test does not distinguish.
ipc_schemas_comment: Added 2026-08-02. This is the runtime half of the frontend's trust boundary (the ts-rs bindings prove the code was BUILT against the right shape, these schemas are what check a given response actually has it), and it carries two decisions with opposite polarity on purpose: validateIpcResult throws on a mismatch (a command result has a caller to reject to), parseEventPayload drops and logs (an event is fire-and-forget and has none). Inverting either is the shape this gate exists to catch. FIRST PASS measured 16.67% total with 9 survivors, which looked like a reason to reject the candidate and was not: reading them is what the protocol above asks for, and all nine were in `describeIssues`, the diagnostic string, while the polarity mutants were already killed. That string is the only record of WHICH field failed (the user sees a generic message by design, so a bug report is the log line), so it was pinned rather than accepted: 91.67% total / 91.67% covered, 11 killed, 1 survivor. The survivor replaces a console.error argument with an empty string and no assertion can reach it, the unobservable-log class the Rust gate excludes by name. The whole file measures identically to its validation block alone: the ~380 lines of zod declarations above are module-level, so `ignoreStatic` skips them, and what the typescript checker does not reject the `satisfies z.ZodType<TauriCommandReturns[K]>` typing does. The glob is therefore the file rather than a range.
tauri_client_comment: MEASURED AND DEFERRED, recorded so the next person does not re-measure it. src/lib/tauri-client.ts is the other half of the seam and scored 25.00% total / 100.00% covered on 2026-08-02: 2 killed, 0 survivors, 6 mutants with NO COVERAGE. Zero survivors is why it is not a gap in the tests that exist, and the 25% is why it is not in the list: every uncovered mutant sits inside `streamLiveChatFile`, whose test does exist, so this is perTest failing to attribute coverage rather than an untested function, the same misattribution the library-folder-section note above warns about, in the other direction. Adding it today would put six permanently-uncovered mutants in the report and teach whoever reads it to skip that file. Find out why the attribution is lost first. The entry can then go in on its own numbers.
coverageAnalysis_comment: Measured on this repo: the mutate globs above yield 6325 mutants. Under the previous 'off' setting each one re-ran the whole 1278-test suite, which put a full run far past the scheduled job's timeout. So the gate never produced a score at all and the break threshold below was moot. 'perTest' runs only the tests that cover each mutant (verified working with the vitest runner).
ignoreStatic_comment: Stryker's own recommendation for this tree: it reports 92 static mutants (1% of the total) estimated to take 58% of the run. A static mutant lives in module-level code, so perTest cannot attribute it to a test and falls back to running the whole suite (the exact cost perTest exists to remove). Skipping that 1% buys back most of the runtime. A full run then takes ~29 minutes locally.
dryRunTimeoutMinutes_comment: Stryker's default is 5 minutes, and the dry run outgrew it: it executes the whole instrumented suite once while the TypeScript checker processes compile in parallel, so it is far slower than the 55s a bare `vitest run` takes. A local run on 12 cores timed out here on 2026-08-01 at 6633 mutants / 1707 tests, before producing any score at all. That failure mode is the reason this is set rather than left to the default. A dry-run timeout aborts the run with no score, which reads in the scheduled job exactly like a mutation-score regression while having nothing to do with test strength. Sized well clear of the observed time rather than just above it, because the number that matters is the one on the slowest machine that ever runs this, not this one.
thresholds_comment: break is what fails the scheduled run (.github/workflows/mutation.yml). Re-measured on CI on 2026-08-01 at 6633 mutants: 73.32%, up from the 71.66% recorded when break was set to 60. That left 13 points of slack rather than the ~11 the previous note claimed, which is most of the way back to the 21-point gap the move off 50 was meant to close: a gate that far below the reading fails only after a regression nobody would need a gate to notice. 68 keeps ~5 points of headroom, which absorbs the normal drift of adding a module before its tests catch up while still failing on a real loss of test strength. Kept equal to 'low' as before, so the band this config declares and the line that fails the run stay the same number. Re-measure before tightening further, and note the measurement has to come from CI or from a local run that reaches the end: a dry-run timeout aborts with no score at all (see dryRunTimeoutMinutes above), which is not a low score.
